claims.text: Progressive creep in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy nanoscale multilayers is controlled by the evolution of interface-localized chemical short-range order.
Initial chemical short-range order at layer interfaces impedes dislocation motion.
Initial interface short-range order strengthens the multilayer.
Sustained stress disrupts interface short-range order.
Loss of interface short-range order facilitates dislocation glide by reducing barrier strength.
Loss of interface short-range order facilitates dislocation nucleation.
Enhanced dislocation nucleation and glide following short-range-order degradation produce an accelerated creep rate.
The proposed starting coatings consist of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The proposed FCC/BCC multilayers have significant lattice distortion.
The proposed multilayers initially have well-developed chemical short-range order at their interfaces.
Layer-composition modifications can enhance or suppress the initial degree of interface short-range order.
Changing individual layer thickness can alter the initial degree of interface short-range order.
Interface short-range order is sensitive to lattice distortion.
Thinner multilayer specimens will show a higher creep rate than the baseline because their interface short-range order degrades more rapidly.
Compositions engineered for stronger initial short-range order will show a higher time-dependent creep rate than the baseline because that order will degrade more rapidly.
The proposed mechanism should dominate at intermediate elevated temperatures and stresses that permit diffusion and dislocation activity while preserving the multilayer architecture.
At very low temperatures, minimal atomic mobility should suppress the proposed short-range-order-evolution mechanism.
At very high temperatures, structural degradation or alternative deformation mechanisms may supersede the proposed mechanism.
